lessons.title: Short Notes
lessons.notes_html:
Meaning of Economics

Economics is the science which studies human behaviour as a relationship between ends and scarce means which have alternative uses. In simple words, it studies how people meet their unlimited wants with limited resources, and how the problem of choice arises from this scarcity.

Definition of Alfred Marshall

Alfred Marshall defined economics as the study of mankind in the ordinary business of life. He said that economics examines that part of individual and social action which is most closely connected with the attainment and use of the material requisites of well-being. In other words, economics studies how people earn wealth and spend it to increase their material welfare.

Definition of Adam Smith

Adam Smith defined economics as an inquiry into the nature and causes of the wealth of nations. He regarded economics as the science of wealth, which studies how wealth is produced, distributed, exchanged and consumed. His famous book 'The Wealth of Nations' was published in 1776.

Micro and Macro Economics

Micro economics studies the economic behaviour of small units, such as an individual consumer, a firm or an industry, while macro economics studies the economy as a whole, such as national income, total employment and general price level. Micro economics deals with parts, macro economics deals with aggregates.

Material Welfare

Material welfare means the well-being that people obtain from material goods and services, such as food, clothing, housing and other necessities of life. It can be measured in terms of money, because material goods have prices, whereas non-material welfare, such as happiness or peace of mind, cannot be measured in money.

lessons.title: Detailed Notes
lessons.notes_html:
Economics as the Study of Wealth

Adam Smith said that 'Economics is a study of wealth'. He is called the founder of economics, and his book 'The Wealth of Nations' appeared in 1776. By wealth he meant all those material goods which are scarce, have utility and can be exchanged, and he studied how such wealth is produced, distributed, exchanged and consumed in a nation.

Marshall's Definition Explained

Alfred Marshall defined economics as the study of mankind in the ordinary business of life. He explained that economics examines that part of individual and social action which is most closely connected with the attainment and use of the material requisites of well-being. The main points of his definition are: first, economics studies human beings and their daily economic activities, not wealth alone; second, it studies material welfare, that is, the well-being obtained from material goods; and third, wealth is only a means to welfare, not an end in itself. This definition broadened economics from a mere study of wealth to a study of human welfare.

Robbins' Definition Explained

Lionel Robbins defined economics as the science which studies human behaviour as a relationship between ends and scarce means which have alternative uses. The main points of his definition are: first, human wants are unlimited, while the resources to satisfy them are limited; second, resources have alternative uses, so man must choose between them; and third, the economic problem is the problem of choice. Robbins extended the scope of economics to all times and all societies, because scarcity and choice exist everywhere. His definition is considered the most clear and comprehensive definition of economics.

Meaning of Economics in Detail

Economics means the study of how human beings meet their unlimited wants with limited resources. The word economics comes from the Greek word 'Oikonomia', which means household management. In the beginning, economics was regarded as the study of wealth, then Marshall described it as the study of material welfare, and finally Robbins described it as the study of human behaviour under scarcity and choice. Thus economics is a social science which studies production, distribution, exchange and consumption of wealth, and guides man in making the best use of scarce resources.

lessons.notes_html:
Economic Goods

Economic goods are those goods which are scarce in supply, have a price, and can be obtained only by paying for them or by making an effort, such as food, clothing, machinery and houses. They are limited as compared to human wants, so man has to spend money or labour to obtain them.

Free Goods

Free goods are those goods which are available in abundance, have no price, and can be obtained without any effort or payment, such as air, sunlight and water in a river. They are unlimited in supply as compared to wants, so no economic problem arises about them.

Meaning of Utility

Utility means the power or quality of a good by which it satisfies a human want. For example, food has utility because it satisfies hunger, and a book has utility because it satisfies the want of knowledge. A good has no economic importance unless it possesses utility.

Meaning of Scarcity

Scarcity means that resources are limited as compared to human wants, which are unlimited. Because of scarcity, man cannot satisfy all his wants at the same time, so he has to make a choice between different wants. Scarcity is the root of all economic problems.

Kinds of Wealth

The four kinds of wealth are: individual wealth, which includes all material things a person possesses, such as a car, clothes and a house; public wealth, which is the property of a country, such as government buildings, roads and railways; national wealth, which includes natural resources such as rivers, mountains, minerals and natural gas; and international wealth, which includes air, ocean and space.

lessons.title: Detailed Notes
lessons.notes_html:
Human Wants: Degrees and Kinds

Human wants mean the desires of man which he wishes to satisfy, such as the want of food, clothing and shelter. Wants have three degrees: necessaries, such as food and clothing, without which life is impossible; comforts, such as a good house and conveyance, which make life easy; and luxuries, such as ornaments and costly goods, which make life luxurious. Wants are also of different kinds: economic and non-economic, individual and collective, and present and future wants.

Utility and Its Importance

Utility in economics means the power of a good to satisfy a human want. Its importance is that man tries to obtain only that good which has utility, and the value and price of a good depend on its utility. An important feature of utility is the law of diminishing marginal utility, which states that the utility obtained from every additional unit of a good goes on decreasing. This principle helps in understanding consumer behaviour and the determination of prices.

Value and Its Determinants

Value means the importance which man attaches to a good, and it is expressed in the form of its price. The factors that determine value are: utility of the good, that is, how much satisfaction it gives; scarcity of the good, that is, how limited its supply is; transferability, that is, whether it can be passed from one person to another; and its price, which is determined by demand and supply. A good with higher value generally commands a higher price.

Value and Price

Value and price are closely related to each other. Value is the importance of a good, while price is the value of a good expressed in terms of money. A good with higher value will have a higher price, because people are willing to pay more for a good that gives them greater satisfaction. In economics, therefore, there is a close relationship among utility, value and price: utility represents value, and value is expressed as price in the market.

lessons.title: Key Facts

Key Points

  • If the price of a good decreases, the quantity demanded increases.
  • The demand curve slopes downward to the right.
  • The law of demand does not hold for inferior, precious and scarce goods.
  • With an increase in the price of a good, the demand for its substitutes increases.
  • When price of a good increases its quantity demanded decreases.
  • With a decrease in the price of inferior goods demand decreases.
  • With an increase in the price of a prestigious goods its demand increases.
  • A change in quantity demanded due to a change in price is called elasticity.

lessons.title: Short Notes
lessons.notes_html:
Definition of Demand

Demand means the quantity of a good which a consumer is willing and able to buy at a given price in a given period of time. Mere desire is not demand; for demand, desire must be combined with the power to buy and the willingness to spend. For example, a poor man may desire a car, but it is not his demand unless he can pay for it.

Functional Equation of Demand

The functional equation of demand shows the relationship between the quantity demanded of a good and the factors that affect it. It is written as Dx = f(Px, Ps, Pc, Y, T, E), where Dx is the quantity demanded of good X, Px is its own price, Ps and Pc are the prices of substitutes and complements, Y is the income of the consumer, T is his taste, and E stands for his expectations about future prices.

Elasticity of Demand

Elasticity of demand means the degree of responsiveness of the quantity demanded of a good to a change in its price. If a small change in price causes a large change in the quantity demanded, demand is said to be elastic; if the quantity demanded changes only slightly, demand is inelastic. Elasticity is measured as the percentage change in quantity demanded divided by the percentage change in price.

Slope of the Demand Curve

The slope of a demand curve is negative, which means that the curve slopes downward from left to right. This shows the inverse relationship between price and quantity demanded: when price rises, quantity demanded falls, and when price falls, quantity demanded rises. That is why the demand curve is drawn falling towards the right.

Other Things Remaining Constant

'Other things remain constant' in the law of demand means that the law applies only when all factors other than the price of the good itself, such as the consumer's income, his taste, the prices of related goods and population, remain unchanged. If these factors change, the demand curve itself shifts its position, and the simple inverse relationship between price and quantity demanded no longer holds.

lessons.title: Detailed Notes
lessons.notes_html:
Law of Demand and Its Assumptions

The law of demand states that, other things remaining constant, the quantity demanded of a good rises when its price falls, and falls when its price rises. Its assumptions are: the prices of related goods do not change, the income and taste of the consumer remain the same, there is no change in population, and the good is a normal good, not an inferior or prestigious good. Under these assumptions, price and quantity demanded move in opposite directions.

Law of Demand: Schedule and Diagram

The law of demand can be explained with the help of a demand schedule and a demand curve. A demand schedule is a table showing different prices of a good and the quantities demanded at those prices, for example: at price 10 the quantity demanded is 100 units, at price 20 it is 80 units, and at price 30 it is 60 units. When these price-quantity pairs are plotted on a diagram, with price on the vertical axis and quantity on the horizontal axis, the points join to form the demand curve, which slopes downward from left to right, showing the inverse relationship between price and quantity demanded.

Law of Demand and Its Limitations

The law of demand means that, other things remaining constant, there is an inverse relationship between the price of a good and its quantity demanded. Its limitations are: it does not apply to inferior goods, whose demand falls when price falls; it does not apply to prestigious or precious goods, whose demand rises when price rises; it does not apply when consumers expect further changes in price; and it fails when the quality of the good changes, as with a new model of a good.

Factors That Change the Quantity Demanded

The factors other than price that bring changes in the quantity demanded are: the income of the consumer, because richer consumers buy more; the prices of related goods, because a rise in the price of a substitute increases demand for the good; the taste and fashion of consumers; the size of population; expectations about future prices; and changes in the quality of the good, as when an improved model increases its demand without any change in price. These factors shift the whole demand curve instead of causing a movement along it.

Meaning of Supply

Supply means the quantity of a good which a producer is willing and able to offer for sale at a given price in a given period of time. It is not the total stock of the good, but only that part of the stock which the producer actually brings to the market for sale at a particular price.

Stock and Supply

Stock means the total quantity of a good available with the producer at a point of time, while supply means only that part of the stock which is actually offered for sale at a given price. For example, if a farmer has 100 bags of wheat in store but offers only 40 bags for sale at the current price, his stock is 100 bags but his supply is 40 bags. Generally, supply is a part of stock.

Supply Schedule

A supply schedule represents a table showing different prices of a good and the quantities supplied at those prices. For example, at price 10 the quantity supplied may be 50 units, at price 20 it may be 80 units, and at price 30 it may be 110 units. The schedule shows the direct relationship between price and quantity supplied, which is then drawn as the upward-sloping supply curve.

lessons.title: Detailed Notes

Law of Supply: Schedule and Diagram

The law of supply states that, other things remaining constant, the quantity supplied of a good rises when its price rises, and falls when its price falls. A supply schedule shows this directly: for example, at price 10 the quantity supplied is 50 units, at price 20 it is 80 units, and at price 30 it is 110 units. lessons.title: Short Notes
lessons.notes_html:
Market Equilibrium

Market equilibrium means the situation in which the quantity demanded of a good is exactly equal to the quantity supplied at a given price. At this point there is neither excess demand nor excess supply, so the price has no tendency to change, and the market is said to be in a stable position.

Equilibrium Price

Equilibrium price is the price at which the quantity demanded of a good equals the quantity supplied. It is determined by the intersection of the demand curve and the supply curve, and at this price the plans of buyers and sellers match each other exactly.

Intersection of Demand and Supply

The intersection of the supply and demand curves determines the equilibrium price and the equilibrium quantity of the good. The point where the downward-sloping demand curve meets the upward-sloping supply curve shows the price at which the market clears and the quantity that is actually bought and sold.

Market Equilibrium: Schedule and Diagram

Market equilibrium can be explained with the help of a schedule and a diagram. A schedule shows different prices and the quantities demanded and supplied at each price, for example: at price 10 the quantity demanded is 100 units and the quantity supplied is 50 units, so there is excess demand; at price 30 the quantity demanded is 50 units and the quantity supplied is 100 units, so there is excess supply; but at price 20 both demand and supply are 75 units, so the market is in equilibrium. On a diagram, the demand curve DD slopes downward from left to right and the supply curve SS slopes upward from left to right, and the point where they intersect shows the equilibrium price and equilibrium quantity.

Equilibrium Price and Quantity

Equilibrium price is the price at which quantity demanded equals quantity supplied, and equilibrium quantity is the amount actually bought and sold at that price. On a diagram, the demand curve slopes downward and the supply curve slopes upward, and their intersection point E shows the equilibrium price on the vertical axis and the equilibrium quantity on the horizontal axis. If the price is set above equilibrium, supply exceeds demand and the price falls; if it is set below equilibrium, demand exceeds supply and the price rises, until the market returns to the intersection point.

lessons.title: Short Notes
lessons.notes_html:
Land

Land means all the natural resources provided free by nature, such as soil, rivers, forests, minerals and climate, which are used in production. Land is a free gift of nature, its supply is limited, and it earns rent as its reward.

Labour

Labour means the physical and mental effort of man used in the production of goods and services. Labour is a living factor of production, it cannot be separated from the labourer, and it earns wages as its reward.

Capital

Capital means that part of man's wealth which is used for producing more wealth, such as machinery, tools, buildings and raw materials. Capital is man-made, it is the result of saving, and it earns interest as its reward.

Organization

Organization means the factor of production which brings land, labour and capital together and takes the risk of production. The organizer, or entrepreneur, decides what, where, how and for whom to produce, combines the other factors in the best proportion, and earns profit as his reward.

Price Changes in the Daily Market

Price changes in daily market because the supply of goods in a daily market, such as vegetables and fish, is fixed for the day and cannot be increased at once. When demand for such goods rises, the price rises, and when demand falls, the price falls, so the price changes daily according to the demand of the day.

lessons.title: Detailed Notes
lessons.notes_html:
Market and Its Kinds

Market means a place or arrangement where buyers and sellers meet for the exchange of goods and services. With regard to the nature of competition, markets are of two kinds: perfect market, in which there are a large number of buyers and sellers, the goods are homogeneous, there is one price for the same good, and no single buyer or seller can influence the price; and imperfect market, in which these conditions do not hold, prices of the same good differ, and sellers can influence prices.

Perfect and Imperfect Markets

In a perfect market there are a large number of buyers and sellers, the goods are homogeneous, there is free entry and exit of firms, the factors of production are mobile, and one price rules for the same commodity. In an imperfect market, on the other hand, the number of buyers and sellers is limited, goods differ in quality, prices of the same good differ from place to place, and individual sellers can influence the price by their own action. Thus perfect competition is a rule of one price, while imperfect competition allows different prices.

Short and Long Period Markets

In a short period market, some factors of production, such as land, are fixed, while others, such as labour, can be changed, and supply can be increased only to a limited extent, so price is influenced mainly by demand. In a long period market, all factors of production become variable, supply can be fully adjusted to demand, and price settles at its normal level, covering the cost of production. The daily market is an even shorter case, in which supply is completely fixed for the day and price changes daily with demand.

Importance of the Factors of Production

The factors of production are land, labour, capital and organization, and each is important in its own way. Land provides the natural resources and raw materials, labour provides the human effort, capital provides the machinery and tools that make production possible on a large scale, and organization combines all the other factors and bears the risk of production. Without any one of these factors, production cannot take place, and the progress of a country depends on the proper combination of all four.

Role of Capital in Production

Capital plays a very important role in production. It provides the machinery, tools and buildings without which modern large-scale production is impossible, and it increases the productivity of labour by giving the worker better equipment. Capital also makes it possible to use natural resources, to adopt new technology, and to carry on production during the long period between investment and the sale of the product. A country with more capital can produce more goods, provide more employment and develop faster.

Per Capita Income

Per capita income means the average income of a person in a country, obtained by dividing the total national income by the total population of the country. It shows the average standard of living of the people, and a low per capita income means that the people of the country are poor on average.

Reasons of Population Growth

Three reasons of population growth in Pakistan are: first, a high birth rate, because of early marriages and a lack of family planning; second, a fall in the death rate, because of better medical facilities and health care; and third, illiteracy and social customs, which discourage small families and encourage large ones.

lessons.notes_html:
Problems of the Agriculture Sector

The problems being faced by agriculture sector in Pakistan are: shortage of water and poor irrigation, small and divided holdings, lack of good seed and fertilizer, difficulty in obtaining loans for farmers, and the effects of changing weather. To solve them, dams should be built and irrigation improved, farmers should be given cheap loans and good seed, agricultural research should be promoted, and access to markets should be made easy so that the farmer gets a fair price for his produce.

Industrial Backwardness

Industrial backwardness in Pakistan means that the industrial sector of the country is under-developed as compared to developed countries. Its causes are shortage of energy, costly raw material, old machinery, lack of skilled labour and lack of investment. Because of industrial backwardness, the country cannot produce enough goods for its own needs, depends on imports, and provides fewer jobs, so removing it is necessary for economic development.

Illiteracy: Reasons and Remedies

The reasons of illiteracy in Pakistan are poverty, because poor parents send their children to work instead of school; lack of schools, especially in rural areas; shortage of trained teachers; and social customs, which keep girls away from education. Its remedial measures are: compulsory and free primary education, opening more schools in villages, training and appointment of teachers, adult literacy programmes, and special attention to the education of women, who form more than half of the population.

Reasons for Population Growth

The reasons for population growth in Pakistan are a high birth rate, a falling death rate due to better health facilities, early marriages, illiteracy, and social and religious customs that favour large families. Poverty also encourages large families, because children are regarded as earning hands. Unless these causes are removed through education and family planning, the population will keep growing faster than resources.

Controlling the Population Growth Rate

The suggestions to control population growth rate are: spread of education, especially female education, because educated families prefer small families; provision of family planning facilities and health services in every area; raising the age of marriage through law; creating employment opportunities, especially for women, so that they take part in economic development; and discouraging social customs that favour large families through public awareness campaigns.

Causes of Low Per Capita Income

The causes of low per capita income in Pakistan are: rapid population growth, which divides the national income among more people; backwardness of agriculture and industry, which keeps production low; illiteracy and lack of skilled labour, which reduce productivity; shortage of capital and energy; and dependence on imports, which drains foreign exchange. Because of these causes, the total income of the country grows slowly while the population grows fast, so the income per person remains low.

lessons.title: Short Notes
lessons.notes_html:
Personal Income

Personal income means the total income actually received by a person from all sources in a year, such as wages, rent, interest and profit, before the payment of direct taxes. It includes transfer payments, such as scholarships and pensions, but it is less than national income, because some income, like undistributed company profits, is not received by persons.

GDP and GNP

Gross domestic product means the money value of all final goods and services produced within the geographical boundaries of a country in a year, while gross national product means the money value of all final goods and services produced by the nationals of the country, including their income earned abroad and excluding the income of foreigners within the country. Thus GNP equals GDP plus net factor income from abroad.

Net National Product

Net national product means the gross national product minus depreciation allowances, that is, the amount spent on the repair and maintenance of plant and machinery. It shows the actual addition to the national income of the country after providing for the wear and tear of capital goods.

Income and Transfer Payments

Income means the reward received for rendering a productive service, such as wages for labour and rent for land, while transfer payments mean payments received without rendering any service, such as Zakat, gifts, scholarships and unemployment allowances. Income is a payment for a service, whereas a transfer payment is a one-sided payment with no service in return.

Disposable Personal Income

Disposable personal income means the personal income left with a person after the payment of direct taxes, which he can spend or save as he likes. It is the income actually available for consumption and saving, and it is less than personal income by the amount of direct taxes paid to the government.

lessons.title: Detailed Notes
lessons.notes_html:
Concept of National Income

National income means the money value of all final goods and services produced in a country in a year, together with the total income earned by the factors of production in that period. It is the sum of wages, rent, interest and profit, and it is always equal to the money value of goods and services produced. National income is the most important measure of the economic progress of a country, because a rising national income means rising production and a higher standard of living.

Various Concepts of National Income

The various concepts of national income are: gross domestic product, which is the value of production within the country; gross national product, which adds net income from abroad; net national product, which is GNP minus depreciation; national income, which is NNP minus indirect taxes plus subsidies; personal income, which is the income actually received by persons; and disposable personal income, which is personal income minus direct taxes. Each concept shows a different stage between total production and the income actually available to the people.

Per Capita Income, Transfer Payments and Depreciation

Per capita income means the national income divided by the total population, and it represents the average standard of living of the people. Transfer payments, such as Zakat and unemployment allowances, have great economic significance because they support the poor and needy without any service in return and reduce inequality. Depreciation allowances are also significant, because the amount set aside for the repair and replacement of machinery keeps the capital stock of the country intact and makes production possible in the future.

Consumption, Savings and Investment

Consumption means the use of goods and services for the satisfaction of wants, savings mean the part of income which is not spent on consumption, and investment means the use of savings for the production of more goods, such as buying machinery or building a factory. Their relationship is that income is either consumed or saved, and savings are invested to increase production; for example, a man earning 100 rupees may spend 70 on consumption, save 30, and invest the 30 in a small business, which increases his future income. Thus consumption, savings and investment are linked: savings make investment possible, and investment increases future consumption.

lessons.title: Short Notes
lessons.notes_html:
Crowther's Definition of Money

G. Crowther defined money as anything that is generally acceptable as a means of exchange and that acts as a measure and a store of value. The important features of his definition are: first, general acceptability, because money is accepted by everyone in exchange; second, it works as a medium of exchange, removing the difficulties of the barter system; and third, it works as a measure of value and a store of value, so wealth can be kept for the future.

Paper Money

Paper money means the currency notes issued by the central bank of a country, which are accepted by everyone in payment because the law declares them legal tender. Paper money has no value of its own as paper, but its face value is greater than its real value, and it circulates because people have faith in the issuing authority and the government.

Convertible and Inconvertible Paper Money

Convertible paper money is that paper money which can be exchanged on demand for gold or silver coins of equal value, while inconvertible paper money cannot be exchanged for gold or silver and circulates only on the faith of the government. Convertible money is backed by metallic reserves, whereas inconvertible money is backed only by law and public confidence.

Value of Money

Value of money means the purchasing power of money, that is, the quantity of goods and services that one unit of money can buy. When prices rise, the value of money falls, because the same amount of money buys fewer goods; and when prices fall, the value of money rises. Thus the value of money and the general price level move in opposite directions.

lessons.title: Detailed Notes
lessons.notes_html:
Barter System and Its Difficulties

Barter system means the direct exchange of goods for goods without the use of money, for example, exchanging wheat for cloth. The difficulties faced by this system are: lack of double coincidence of wants, because the wheat owner must find a cloth owner who wants wheat; difficulty in measuring value, because there is no common measure; difficulty in dividing goods, because a cow cannot be divided for small exchanges; difficulty in storing wealth; and difficulty in making deferred payments and transporting goods.

Money: Definition and Features

Money is anything that is generally acceptable as a medium of exchange and as a measure and store of value. Its important features are: general acceptability by everyone; it works as a medium of exchange and removes barter difficulties; it is a measure of value, so the prices of all goods can be compared; it is a store of value, so wealth can be saved for the future; and it makes deferred payments and the transfer of wealth easy.

Functions of Money

The functions of money are: medium of exchange, because goods are bought and sold for money instead of direct barter; measure of value, because the price of every good is expressed in money; store of value, because money can be saved for future use; standard of deferred payments, because loans and wages are fixed in money; and transfer of wealth, because money can be easily carried from one place to another. For example, a farmer sells his wheat for money, keeps the money, and later buys cloth with it.

Kinds of Money

The kinds of money are: credit money, which consists of cheques, drafts, hundies and credit cards issued by banks and depends on the credit of the bank; near money, which includes postal certificates and prize bonds that can be quickly converted into money; paper money, which consists of currency notes issued by the central bank and accepted as legal tender; metallic money, which consists of coins made of gold, silver, nickel or copper; and token money, whose face value is greater than the value of the metal or paper it contains, such as small coins and notes.

Factors Causing Changes in the Value of Money

The factors causing changes in the value of money are: the quantity of money, because an increase in its supply raises prices and lowers its value; the volume of production, because more goods against the same money raise its value; the velocity of circulation, because faster spending raises prices; the demand for money, because higher demand raises its value; and changes in population, taxes, and government expenditure, which affect prices. In short, the value of money depends on the demand for and supply of money in relation to goods.

Principles of Note Issuing

The principles of note issuing are: first, the currency system, which requires that notes be issued under a proper system, such as the proportional reserve system; second, the security principle, which requires that the central bank keep sufficient reserves against the notes issued; and third, the elasticity principle, which requires that the supply of notes can be increased or decreased according to the needs of trade. These principles keep the currency stable and trustworthy.

Central Bank as Banker to the State

The central bank is called banker to the state because it acts as the banker of the government: it keeps government deposits, makes payments on behalf of the government, manages the public debt, and advises the government on monetary matters. Just as a commercial bank serves the public, the central bank serves the state in all its banking business.

Bank Rate Policy

Bank rate policy means the policy of the central bank to control credit by changing the bank rate, which is the rate at which the central bank advances loans to commercial banks. When the bank rate is raised, loans become costly, credit contracts and prices fall; when it is lowered, loans become cheap, credit expands and business activity increases. Thus bank rate policy is a tool for controlling the money supply.

lessons.notes_html:
Commercial Bank and Its Functions

A commercial bank is an institution which accepts deposits from the public and advances loans to traders, industrialists and farmers. Its functions are: accepting deposits in current, saving and fixed accounts; advancing loans and overdrafts; transferring money from one place to another; collecting cheques and bills on behalf of customers; issuing credit instruments like drafts; and providing safe custody of valuables. Commercial banks thus collect the scattered savings of the people and make them available for trade and industry.

Kinds of Banks

The important kinds of banks are: central bank, which issues currency and controls credit; commercial banks, which accept deposits and advance loans; industrial banks, which provide long-term loans to industries; agricultural banks, which provide loans to farmers; and savings banks, which encourage small savings of the people. Each kind serves a different part of the economy, but all of them deal in money and credit.

Central Bank and Its Functions

The central bank is the apex bank of a country, which issues currency notes, controls credit and acts as banker to the government and to the commercial banks. Its functions are: monopoly of note issue; banker to the government; bankers' bank, keeping the reserves of commercial banks; controller of credit and money supply; custodian of foreign exchange reserves; and clearing house for commercial banks. The State Bank of Pakistan performs all these functions in our country.

How the Central Bank Controls Credit

The central bank controls credit money as the controller of money supply by using the bank rate, open market operations and the reserve ratio. By raising the bank rate and selling securities, it makes loans costly and contracts credit; by lowering the bank rate and buying securities, it makes loans cheap and expands credit. By raising the cash reserve ratio of commercial banks, it reduces their power to lend, and by lowering it, it increases their lending power. In this way the central bank keeps the money supply according to the needs of the economy.

Interest-Free Banking in Pakistan

The steps taken for the success of interest free banking in Pakistan are: the introduction of profit and loss sharing in 1981, under which banks share profit and loss with depositors instead of paying interest; the mode of modaraba, under which the bank provides capital and the borrower provides skill; the mode of musharaka, under which both bank and borrower share capital and profit; interest free loans with service charges, usually for exporters; and qarz-e-hasna, interest free loans for the needy, especially students, for educational expenses. The government amended the relevant laws so that the banking system works according to the teachings of Islam.

Disadvantages of International Trade

Three disadvantages of international trade are: first, dependence on foreign countries, which is harmful in times of war; second, local industries suffer because of competition with cheaper foreign goods; and third, the balance of trade usually remains in deficit, which drains the foreign exchange reserves of the country.

Domestic and International Trade

Domestic trade means trade within the boundaries of one country, between different cities and regions, in the same currency and under the same laws, with free mobility of labour and capital. International trade means trade between different countries, in different currencies and under different laws, with restrictions on the movement of labour and capital and with payments through foreign exchange. Thus domestic trade is simple and free, while international trade faces legal, currency and transport difficulties.

Advantages and Disadvantages of International Trade

The advantages of international trade are: availability of goods not produced at home, specialization which lowers costs, larger markets for producers, better quality through competition, and earning of foreign exchange. Its disadvantages are: dependence on other countries, harm to local industries from foreign competition, deficit in the balance of trade, and the danger that political differences may stop the supply of essential goods. On balance, international trade is useful if it is managed so that its disadvantages are kept under control.

Balance of Trade and Balance of Payments

Balance of trade means the difference between the value of visible goods exported and imported by a country, while balance of payments means the comprehensive record of all economic transactions, visible and invisible, between the residents of one country and foreign countries. Balance of trade covers only goods, whereas balance of payments also covers services, interest, gifts and capital movements, so the balance of payments is a wider concept than the balance of trade.

Important Imports and Exports of Pakistan

The important imports of Pakistan are petroleum and its products, because the country lacks oil resources; eatables such as tea, edible oil and sugar; chemical goods needed by industries; machinery and raw material needed for industrial development; iron, steel and chemical fertilizers. The important exports of Pakistan are cotton and cotton cloth, which hold the top position; carpets, famous for hand-knotted quality; leather and its products; and other items such as surgical goods, sports goods and ready-made garments. Pakistan's balance of trade usually remains in deficit, because imports exceed exports.

lessons.notes_html:
Public Finance

Public finance means the study of the revenue and expenditure of the government and the management of public debt. It studies how the government collects its income through taxes and other sources, how it spends that income on defence, administration and welfare, and how it covers its deficit when expenditure exceeds revenue.

Private Finance

Private finance means the finance of individuals and private institutions, in which a person cuts his coat according to his cloth, that is, he adjusts his expenditure according to his income. Unlike the government, a private person cannot print currency notes or borrow without limit, and he must keep his expenditure within his income.

Public Finance and Private Finance

Two points of difference between public and private finance are: first, the government adjusts its income according to its expenditure, while a private person adjusts his expenditure according to his income; and second, the government can print currency notes and borrow on a large scale, while a private person cannot do so.

Sources of Public Revenue

Five sources of public revenue are: taxes, such as income tax and sales tax; fees charged for government services; fines imposed for breaking laws, such as wrong parking; profits of government enterprises; and miscellaneous revenues, such as royalties, grants and gifts from foreign governments.

Public Debt

Public debt means the money borrowed by a government to make up its deficit. It comprises all loans obtained by a government to finance its requirements, including defence, trade and commerce, exploration of natural resources and social development projects. The government has to pay interest as well as the principal amount of these loans.

lessons.title: Detailed Notes
lessons.notes_html:
Public and Private Finance: Differences

Public finance differs from private finance in several ways: the government adjusts its income to its expenditure, while a private person adjusts his expenditure to his income; the government can print notes and borrow heavily, while a person cannot; the government spends for public welfare and not for profit, while a person spends for his own benefit; and the government budget is usually a deficit budget, while a private budget is usually balanced. These differences arise because the aims and powers of the government are different from those of an individual.

Public and Private Finance: Similarities

The similarities between public and private finance are: both deal with income and expenditure; both try to keep a balance between income and expenditure; both borrow when income falls short; and both aim at maximum welfare, the government for the public and the individual for his family. In both cases, a deficit causes difficulties and a surplus provides relief.

Sources of Public Revenue

The sources of public revenue are: taxes, which are compulsory payments, such as income tax, sales tax and customs duties; fees for government services; fines for breaking laws; income from government property and enterprises; and miscellaneous sources, such as royalties, grants and gifts from foreign governments and organizations. All these resources are used for the collective social welfare of the general public.

Heads of Public Expenditure

The major heads of public expenditure are: defence, which takes a major portion of revenue for strengthening national defence; debt servicing, which is the payment of interest and principal on loans; courts and judiciary, for the supremacy of law; administration, for paying government employees and running departments; and miscellaneous expenditure, for basic amenities such as education, healthcare, drinking water and communication. Defence expenditure is one of the major parts of government spending.

Budget and Public Debt

Budget means the annual statement of the estimated revenue and expenditure of the government for one year, from 1st July to 30th June of the next year. It is also called an estimate, because it estimates the income and spending of the coming year. Public debt means the money borrowed by the government to cover its deficit, for reasons such as completing development projects, meeting emergencies like floods and earthquakes, and covering the deficit in the balance of payments. The government pays interest and principal on this debt from its revenue.

lessons.title: Short Notes

Meaning of Economic Development

Economic development means the process by which the real national income of a country increases over a long period of time and the standard of living of the people rises. It is not merely an increase in income, but also includes improvement in education, health, employment and basic infrastructure.

Economic Factors of Development

The names of economic factors of economic development are: capital, natural resources, technology, skilled labour and entrepreneurship. These factors increase production and productivity, and their proper use speeds up the rate of economic development.

Importance of the Industrial Sector

The industrial sector is important in Pakistan because it provides employment opportunities, produces goods for exports, converts agricultural raw material into useful products, and contributes about 21 percent to the national income. Industries increase the self-reliance of the country and speed up the rate of economic development.

Importance of the Agriculture Sector

The agriculture sector is important for Pakistan because it contributes about 19 percent of the national production, provides employment to a large part of the population, supplies raw material to industries, such as cotton to the textile industry, and meets the food needs of the country. That is why agriculture is called the backbone of Pakistan's economy.

Role of Technology in Development

The role of technology in the economic development of Pakistan is that modern machines and methods increase production and reduce cost; in agriculture, new seed and irrigation methods increase output; in industries, automatic systems improve quality; and means of communication and the internet make trade and access to information easy. Technology therefore speeds up the rate of development.

lessons.title: Detailed Notes
lessons.notes_html:
Definition of Economic Development

Economic development means the long-term process in which the real national income and per capita income of a country increase continuously, and along with it the standard of living, education, health and employment of the people also improve. According to Meier and Baldwin, economic development is the process by which real national income increases over a long period of time.

Factors Affecting Economic Development

The factors affecting economic development are: economic factors, such as supply of capital, use of natural resources, technology and skilled labour, which increase production; political factors, such as stability of government, law and order and good economic policies, which promote investment; and social factors, such as education, health, population growth and social traditions, which affect the productivity of labour and the habit of saving.

Role of Agriculture in Development

The role of the agriculture sector in the economic development of Pakistan is that it is the backbone of the economy, contributing about 19 percent of production and employing a large part of the population. It supplies raw material to industries and food to the people, and its progress increases the income of farmers, which increases the demand for industrial goods. The development of agriculture therefore promotes the development of the whole economy.

Industrial Sector and Economic Growth

The industrial sector is helping in achieving economic growth in Pakistan by providing employment, producing goods for exports and earning foreign exchange, and converting agricultural raw material into finished goods. Industries increase national income, make the country self-reliant, and raise the standard of living. However, the industrial sector still faces problems of energy shortage, costly raw material and old machinery, which must be removed by new energy sources, cheap loans and technical education.

Role of Trade and Banking

The role of trade in the economic development of Pakistan is that exports earn foreign exchange, imports provide necessary machinery and raw material, and competition improves the quality of local industries. The role of banking is that banks collect savings and advance loans to industry and agriculture, promote investment, and make the transfer of money easy. Without trade and banking, the rate of economic development remains slow.

Communication and Modern Technology

Means of communication and modern technology are essential for economic development because means of communication, such as radio, television, internet and print media, spread information quickly, give farmers and traders knowledge of prices and markets, and increase education and awareness. Modern technology increases production, reduces cost, creates new industries and makes the country able to compete in the world. That is why both are indispensable for development.

Meaning of Zakat

Zakat means the fixed amount of wealth which a sahib-e-nisab Muslim pays to the deserving persons after the passing of a year, under the command of Allah. It is a financial worship, its rate is generally two and a half percent, and its purpose is to keep wealth in circulation and to reduce poverty.

Characteristics of the Islamic Economic System

Five characteristics of the Islamic economic system are: first, the right of private ownership, but as a trust from Allah; second, prohibition of interest; third, fair distribution of wealth through Zakat and Usher; fourth, discouragement of concentration of wealth and hoarding; and fifth, earning through lawful means and prohibition of unlawful sources of income, such as gambling and speculation.

A Moderate Economic System

The Islamic economic system is called moderate because it adopts a balanced path between the uncontrolled freedom of capitalism and the complete control of socialism. It allows private ownership and also arranges fair distribution of wealth, it gives freedom to the individual and also cares for the welfare of society, so it is called a moderate system.

Zakat against Poverty and Unemployment

Poverty and unemployment can be alleviated by Zakat in this way: the amount of Zakat is given to the poor and unemployed, which meets their basic needs; Zakat helps in starting small businesses, which creates employment; and wealth remains in circulation, which increases production and economic activity. In this way Zakat reduces economic inequality.

lessons.title: Detailed Notes
lessons.notes_html:
Islamic Economic System

The Islamic economic system means the economic system which is based on the teachings of the Quran and Sunnah, and in which all matters of production, distribution, exchange and consumption are carried out according to Islamic principles. In this system Allah is regarded as the real owner of wealth and man is His deputy and trustee, so wealth must be used according to the pleasure of Allah.

Salient Features of the Islamic Economic System

The salient features of the Islamic economic system are: the right of private ownership, but as a trust and within the limits set by Allah; complete prohibition of interest, replaced by banking based on profit and loss sharing; fair distribution of wealth through Zakat, Usher and charity; prohibition of concentration of wealth, hoarding and unlawful sources of income; respect for labour and protection of the rights of workers; and social welfare, meaning that meeting the basic needs of every person is the responsibility of the state.

Zakat and Its Recipients

Zakat means the financial worship obligatory on a sahib-e-nisab Muslim, in which he pays a fixed share of his wealth, generally two and a half percent, to the deserving persons after the passing of a year. The recipients of Zakat are the eight categories stated in the Quran: the poor, the needy, the collectors of Zakat, those whose hearts are to be won, freeing of slaves, debtors, in the way of Allah, and the traveller.

Ending Unemployment through Zakat, Usher and Charity

In a Muslim state, unemployment can be resolved through Zakat, Usher and charity in this way: the amount of Zakat is given to the poor for learning a skill and starting a business, so that they become self-reliant; Usher spends one-tenth of agricultural produce on poor farmers and rural welfare; and charity, that is, voluntary spending in the way of Allah, runs schools, hospitals and employment projects. Through these three sources, wealth reaches the poor, production increases, and poverty and unemployment in society decrease.
